test_title: PYST 38: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 14 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: According to Archimedes’ principle, what is the magnitude of the upward force (buoyant force)?

options.text: It is equal to the pressure exerted by the fluid.
It is equal to the volume of the fluid.
It is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.
It is equal to the weight of the immersed body.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Archimedes' principle** states that when a body is immersed fully or partially in a **fluid**, it experiences an upward force that is equal to the **weight of the fluid displaced** by it.
 
• The upward force mentioned in the principle is known as the **buoyant force** or **upthrust**.
 
• The magnitude of this force depends on the **density of the fluid** and the **volume of the immersed part** of the body. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• While **pressure** exerted by the fluid increases with depth and contributes to the upward force (due to the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the object), the force itself is not numerically equal to the pressure. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The magnitude of the force is equal to the **weight** (a force measured in **Newtons**), not the **volume** (measured in **cubic meters**). Volume determines how much fluid is moved, but the force is the weight of that volume. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **weight of the immersed body** only equals the buoyant force when the object is **floating** in equilibrium. If the object sinks, its weight is greater than the buoyant force. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Buoyancy:** It is the property of a fluid to exert an upward force on any object immersed in it. This phenomenon is why objects feel lighter when submerged in **water**.
 
• **Density:** It is defined as the **mass per unit volume** of a substance. The **SI unit** of density is **kg/m³**. An object will float if its density is less than the density of the liquid.
 
• **Relative Density:** This is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of **water** at **4 degrees Celsius**. Since it is a ratio of similar quantities, it has **no units**.
 
• **Applications of Archimedes' Principle:**
 
 
• **Designing Ships and Submarines:** Used to ensure they displace enough water to stay afloat or submerge as needed.
 
• **Lactometers:** These instruments are used to determine the **purity of a sample of milk** based on its density.
 
• **Hydrometers:** These are used for determining the **density of liquids**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Apparent Weight:** When an object is in a fluid, its **apparent weight** is its actual weight minus the **buoyant force**. This explains why heavy stones are easier to lift while they are still under the water.
 
• **Sinking vs. Floating:**
 
 
• If the **buoyant force** is less than the weight of the object, the object will **sink**.
 
• If the **buoyant force** is equal to or greater than the weight of the object, the object will **float**.
 
 
 
• The principle applies to all **fluids**, which include both **liquids** and **gases**. For example, a **hot air balloon** rises because the weight of the air it displaces is greater than the weight of the balloon itself.
 
• The discovery is attributed to **Archimedes**, a Greek mathematician and inventor from **Syracuse**, in the **3rd century BC**.
